utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go back to Exhibit P463 which was where we were yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, you will recall this is a transcript of a meeting between President Tudjman and Minister Radic on the 22nd of August, 1995. If we could go to page 9 of the English and page 14 in the B/C/S. And yesterday, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, I asked you a question about whether President Tudjman's statement to Mr. Radic that they should charter flights and boats to bring Croats in from Argentina and Australia was a reflection of his desire to fill the empty spaces that existed after Operation Storm with Croats. And you began your answer by stating: "This was a reflection of the situation that required these empty spaces to be filled in, because otherwise they would pose a danger, strategically speaking. This is a very narrow area, facing the Republika Srpska, and if it is void of people, it was possible for the property to be demolished, incursions were possible to take place, and it was absolutely necessary to have people settle there." And I would like to go to one other passage of this transcript, and this is Mr. Radic speaking at the bottom of the page, on both the English and the B/C/S. In the second paragraph of his speech he says: "Now look, I have been looking around this area a bit, the biggest centres where we should focus on return, regarding the national interest. I have tried to make a chronological order or some kind of hierarchy, and in my opinion, I would like to discuss this with you a bit? "The map of the whole area is of a strategic importance for Croatia. I coloured it with different colours. This is what has always been critical for us in the history, not Knin, we'll manage to do that slowly. If you ask me the first ... I defined five priorities according to the urgency of colonizing these places with Croats. If you ask me this thing right here is the first and the second priority ..." I think we should turn the page in the B/C/S. "We should bring Croats back here urgently, and this area should be urgently colonized with Croats. And we should, by no means, let more than 10 percent of Serbs be here ever again. Because that is where we were cut off." And the president says: "Not even 10 percent." And Mr. Radic says: "Okay, I'm talking about 10 percent. So the first priority of colonizing is right here, in my opinion, Petrova and Svenska Gora, that's where we have to establish some kind of a city sooner or later. We also have Vojnic. And Veljun, a somewhat smaller place. And Vojnic is a bigger place. "However, by our companies opening factories, just as the Serbs did in Licki Osijek, I visited that factory. That looks marvellous. They built apartments for 4.000 people, where we can bring people right away. It's just that we don't have anybody." Then there's a conversation between the two, and Mr. Radic picks up on this subject at page 16 of the B/C/S and page 11 of the English. The second paragraph again. Oh, sorry. Halfway through, approximately, the last sentence. "Let me get back to this, our Licki Osijek should be developed with that area as we stimulate the ones who are abroad and the temporary ones as much as we can, so nothing could happen to us here ever again." And the president says: "It will never happen again." When Mr. Radic refers to "nothing happening to us here ever again," he is referring to the things that happened to the Croats between 1991 and 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that is the case. It is difficult to interpret and explain what Mr. Radic meant to say 15 years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the strategy as expressed here, as far as -- as far as you know it is to fill these empty spaces with Croats so that nothing happens to the Croats in that area ever again; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, there were over 150.000 Croats in the area who were expelled in 1991. The intention was to bring these Croats back that had been expelled and to put them in their own houses. It is difficult now to comment on the speech of Mr. Jure Radic. His views an ideas oftentimes were not accepted; some were, some were not. He was the minister for reconstruction and refugees, and he had a very challenging situation to face, when it come to providing accommodation for those people. I'm not saying that all his ideas were wise; quite to the contrary, some of them were not. And as for the statement that you put to me, or, rather, that you quoted me as saying yesterday, concerning president's idea to charter boats and airplanes and fill them with them Croats to bring them to settle in Croatia, I think that this is somehow improperly being attached to what is the main subject of our discussion. Our principal topic was the return of the Croats who had been expelled from those areas. When Tudjman spoke, when Tudjman spoke about them, he often had in mind the Krajina leadership and, hence, these transcripts do not reflect sufficiently the actual situation. I also said yesterday that we had a problem with the accommodation for the refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were coming at the time from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to interrupt you, as I think you have answered my question sufficiently. I just like to go back to what you said at the beginning of your was about Mr. Radic, "his views an ideas oftentimes were not accepted." But isn't the case here that when he says "we should by no means let more than 10 percent of Serbs be here ever again," and the president says "not even 10 percent," President Tudjman is, in fact, accepting Mr. Radic view?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjo Tudjman often had a different story for each of his ministers. It might be that in this conversation he did say that. But we have to look at the context. You have to look at the facial expressions and to -- at everything that transpired between these two. It is difficult to explain because we are looking here only at a transcript. However, none of these things were put into practice later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to move on to -- back to the property law that you gave evidence about yesterday. And you were asked about requirements to sell property under the law on the temporary takeover and administration of property. And your evidence was: "There was no such requirement. There was a possibility for those who did not wish to return to Croatia to sell their property." Isn't the case, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, that this law, in fact, had a general rule which was to prohibit the sale of these properties by the owners?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The law on the temporary takeover of property stated that it was prohibited to sell properties under that law, that the Serb who had left the Krajina could not sell their property. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, the government issued a decree in 1995 on the temporary takeover of the abandoned property. Later on, the Croatian parliament adopted a law which remained in force until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Let's look at that law then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Which is D422. And if we could first look at Article 2, which is on page 1 of the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And paragraph 1 of Article 2 is the one I'm interested in. And that's the provision that put the property of the Serbs who had left the Krajina into the possession of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I object to that a question. I object. I mean, if that's a question, I don't know if it is posed as a question or a statement by counsel. Because if it's a statement by counsel, I object. If it is a question then I think the witness should be given the opportunity to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to look at three provisions of the law and then ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Ms. Gustafson is drawing the attention, and she summarized a certain position and then they'll put questions to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if we could look to Article 5, which, I think, is on the same page in the B/C/S and the next page of the English. And paragraph 1 of this Article refers to the persons -- displaced persons, refugees, returnees, et cetera, to whom this property can be granted for use and possession. This paragraph, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, this is the people who were to benefit from this law, this is the displaced persons in Croatia and the Bosnian Croat refugees you were referring to yesterday. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The people who were supposed to use those houses were those expellees who had lost or whose status of expellee had been cancelled, and they had to go back. However, their houses were demolished and such people were put up temporarily in the abandoned houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could try to just focus your answer on the question I asked, I would appreciate it. Our time is limited.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to Article 11, which is on page 4 of the English and page 3, still, of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 1 of this Article, this is the provision that gave the Serbs who had left the Krajina 90 days to return to the Republic of Croatia and claim their property back. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And finally, if we could go to Article 8, which is on the previous page of the English; same page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it's the first two paragraphs here I'm interested in. The first paragraph says: "As long as the property is administered by the Republic of Croatia, its owner cannot dispose of, meaning alienate, exchange, lease, let for temporary paid or free use, mortgage, or otherwise encumber such property. And under paragraph 2: "The government can, at the proposal of the minister of the justice exempt certain property from this prohibition." Having seen this now, does this remind you of the general prohibition of the sale of property under this law?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot explain at this moment to you these temporary provisions and make a difference between them and permanent provisions. This was the Law on Temporary Takeover and administration, so it was temporary. Therefore, the whole procedure that followed was affected in a way that everyone who claimed their property was either given it or was allowed to sell it or was offered another property somewhere else in Croatia. There were several options offered to both to those who didn't want to come back and those who wanted to come back, and the whole system was in place. Whether it was a good system or a perfect one, it certainly wasn't. But you have to take into account the circumstances and the situation that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, in the spirit of Rule 90(H) of putting the case to the witness and giving a few disclosure to the Trial Chamber as to the rights of all parties, I think the Trial Chamber should instruct the OTP to have the witness look at Article 7 as well, which gives both sides of the equation of the possessor and the owner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Putting the case to the witness, isn't that if it does not deal with the matters raised in-chief but -- let me have a look at Rule 90(H). I haven't got it here at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this provision is irrelevant to the questions I am asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It certainly is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it is something that can be gone into on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Rule 90(H)(i) gives several categories of subject of cross-examination. The first, subject matter of the evidence in chief; second, credibility; third, where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party to the subject matter of that case. That's the third category. I think in (ii) clear reference is made to the third category. What Ms. Gustafson is doing, she is dealing with the subject matter of the evidence in chief. And if you consider other matters to be relevant, that is not what the case is, but whether she has dealt with everything you consider to be relevant, then have you an opportunity to put further questions to the witness at a later stage. Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. At this moment I allow Ms. Gustafson to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, at the appropriate time I would like to put my further comment on the record that I can't put on right now. I can do it at the end of the break or the beginning of the second break, but I would like to put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the break you will have an opportunity to put on the record what you wish to put on the record. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, a few moments ago you said that this law was in place until 1998. And now you've said -- you've talked about these temporary provisions, and there was a whole procedure. But this was the law that governed the administration, use, and disposition of the property of the Krajina Serbs. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it seized to be in effect in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your words were: "Later on" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be, I like to hear French. But channel 4 is not the channel that I expected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your words were -- I'll quote them back to you: "Later on the Croatian parliament adopted law which remained in force until 1998."

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then it seized to be in effect in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be clear, as I said before, let's focus on what we're talking about. We're talking at this moment about this law which was, as the witness said, in force since its adoption, until 1998. If there's -- if we have to pay attention to legislation that came later, we'll do it at this moment; let's not mix up matters. We're now focussing on the law in existence during the period of time Ms. Gustafson is referring to, and the period of time you mentioned. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, there was one further amendment to this law in January of 1996, you may recall. It removed the 90-day limitation and in place it stated that the issue of returning and possession and use of property which is under the ownership --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. If the witness is able to look at the exhibit, which is P475 and put --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking -- this is a preliminary to my question, Your Honour. I don't need to put the witness. I'm limited in my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's first hear what question Ms. Gustafson attaches to it, and if the witness disagrees with anything said, then we'll hear from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, what she's reading is -- what counsel is reading is P457.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Which I was about to inform the Court of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's -- yesterday I urged Ms. Gustafson not to intervene unnecessarily. Let's first wait and see what Ms. Gustafson puts on the record, how she introduces her question, and if there's anything obviously wrong in that, of course, is what she said until now, is that wrong? Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is not -- but you know that is not what I am saying. What I'm saying is the witness should be given an opportunity to look at the document, period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear what Ms. Gustafson's -- says until now, from what I understand from you, she did not represent anything in a wrong way. Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And as I was stating, this amendment remove the 90-day limitation and in place stated that the issue of returning and possession and use of property under the ownership of persons from Article 2 of this law will be regulated by the agreement on the normalisation of relations between Croatia and the FRY. And that is Exhibit P475. Do you recall an amendment in January of 1996? And in fact the law in that form remained in place until September of -- I'm about to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe, let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Ms. Skare Ozbolt, Ms. Gustafson draws your attention to an amendment to the law and she asked you whether you remember that there was an amendment. You answered that question with yes. If, for the purpose of answering any question, you'd like to look at an amendment because Ms. Gustafson is putting questions to you that you couldn't answer, but the only question she has put to you until now is whether it is your recollection that there was an amendment. Apparently you remember that. Now if there is any need to consult any document because you couldn't answer the question without looking at it, keeping in mind what Ms. Gustafson is asking you, please ask for looking at it, but perhaps, first, we wait what the question is, she might ask you whether it was published in the -- in a certain newspaper, or whatever, for which you might not need to consult the text itself. If, however, she goes into details asking you questions and if you feel the need to have a look at that document, of course, you should just ask. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, yesterday you testified that this law at no cost allowed for the confiscation of property because private property is protected in Croatia under the law. And in fact private property is protected in Croatia under the constitution. That's right, isn't it? Including Article 50 of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it's the case, is it not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, you're nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct. Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Overlapping speakers] ... and expression of faces. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And it's the case --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything that you said is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it is also the case that this law was found to be unconstitutional by the Croatian Constitutional Court because it violated Article 50 of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And that is why it was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that was in September of 1997; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little later, I think. But probably, if you have that information, then it's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let's look at that decision. It's D425.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 8 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S. And the paragraph that begins: "Article 50." It's about halfway down the page in the English and the same in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this passage explains that Article 50 of the constitution stipulates that "ownership may be restricted by law in the interest of the Republic ... but only against indemnity equal to its market value."

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "Article 8, paragraphs 1 and 5, of the contested law, restricts the right of ownership but without indemnity." And then if we skip to the next paragraph, the last sentence: "Consequently the court found that Article 8, paragraph 1 and 5, were unconstitutional." Now, this decision represents the truth about this law; namely, that it restricted the right of ownership without indemnity. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I mean, is that testimony by counsel or a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is certainly very leading, which is, of course, in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apart from whether it is the truth about law, this is what apparently the constitutional court established as being the legal position expressed by this judicial organ. Whether you call that truth or -- that what the decision says. And I don't think that Ms. Skare Ozbolt is challenging that this is what the constitutional court said. But if she has any specific comment on it, then, Ms. Gustafson, I take it that you would like to hear from her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I can just ask the question in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Kuzmanovic is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The limitation is specifically limited to Articles 8, paragraphs 1 and 5, so it's not the truth about the law, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... this is it exactly why I want to avoid this kind of conclusion whether this is the truth, truth about what, this is it what the decision says. And if Ms. Skare Ozbolt has any comment to make on this as, for example, later decisions denying or overturning this decision, we'd like to hear from her. Let's stop having this kind of discussions. Of course, the questions will be put by Ms. Gustafson with a certain focus as parties usually do. Ms. Gustafson, as I expressed earlier, the question was phrased not with the accuracy this Chamber likes most. But we're talking about a paragraph in a decision of the constitutional court. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Let me just ask this.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yesterday when you said the law at no cost allowed for the confiscation of property because private property is protected in Croatia under the law, that's not right, is it? This law in fact allowed for the confiscation of property, did it not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to repeat what I already stated yesterday, and that is there was no confiscation of property. There was the temporary seizure of property. The constitutional court characterized parts of this law as anti-constitutional, the provisions of two Articles of this law against the constitution because it did not provide for indemnity for seized property. This was corrected later. And I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that that year the agency for sales of property was formed, and it was pursuant to the agreement for normalisation of relations between Serbia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I rise just for -- to check an interpretation at page 16, line 18, I believe there was an adjective that the witness used with respect to the end of the sentence there. I don't wan to even use the word to be accused of leading her. There's a sentence that ends in line 18. She uses an additional adjective to describe that there, and perhaps we can check with her. Because I think it is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Skare Ozbolt, you also read English. Could you check whether, on the page which is on your screen, page 18 -- line 18 at the end, whether anything is missing in the translation as written. It now reads: "The provisions of two Articles of this law against the constitution, because it did not provide for indemnity for seized property." Anything missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that is the sense, but I really ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll proceed. Mr. Misetic, if there's any need, you know the procedures for having the transcript corrected on the basis of the original. The Chamber, of course, will consider any such -- any such request. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just to clarify that answer, you said this was corrected later. And you said, I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that that year the agency for sales of property was formed. But that year, are you referring to 1997, the same year of this decision?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1998. The normalization of Croatian-Serbian relations took place in 1997, and as part of that, these matters were discussed. In 1998, the agency for the sales of property was formed, and it is still functioning today.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move now to another topic, which is the negotiations in Geneva that you spoke about. And you said in your statement and you repeated in your testimony that: "A yes in Geneva by the Serbs would have meant the implementation of the same model of peaceful reintegration as it was implemented in Eastern Slavonia." And the first question I'd like to ask you about that is in relation to the decision to launch Operation Storm. And in that regard you have emphasised, I think, the importance of the acceptance or refusal of the RSK contingent in Geneva on the 3rd of August. Did you know that there were actually several factors, both military and political, that caused the Croatian leadership and President Tudjman to view the situation on the 3rd of August as a unique opportunity to attack the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm gladly going to tell you what I knew and what I know, but if you can specify which factors are these, the military and political factors that you mean, I will gladly tell you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you gave evidence that there was a meeting of the -- of the VONS of the Defence and Security Council on the 3rd of August and that you came at the end of that meeting with Mr. Pasalic. And at the beginning of that meeting, President Tudjman stated that he had received a call from Mr. Pasalic in Geneva, and he had been told that the Serbs had not accepted, and the talks were over.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is, for the benefit of the Court and the parties, at D1454.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then President Tudjman stated: "As far as I am concerned, I think that we must not abandon our decision because of public opinion and the general situation. It is evident that Serb and the supporters of a peaceful solution do not have the biggest say. There is no unity and that the wrangling would continue on end. "It is also evidence that the present balance of forces and the international political situation are such that we were able to undertake -- that we would be able to undertake that action." Were you aware that President Tudjman was weighing these factors - public opinion, the balance of forces, the international political situation - in coming to this decision?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facts were as follows. The Republic of Serbian Krajina sought, and in some way, wanted to unite with Republika Srpska. At the time 6.000 soldiers and heavy artillery from Serbia arrived in the area of the town of Slunj where they had a military exercise. There was a lot of discord, and it was not possible to talk with anyone any longer in the SAO Krajina leadership. The situation, the economic situation in Croatia in general, included a lot of problems with the people who were expelled, and the situation was very frustrating in a number of parts of Croatia. All of these were elements in deciding about the Storm action, not to speak about the broader context of the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And a little later in that meeting, Mr. Granic - who was the foreign minister; is that right - says: "We will not have an another" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. It may be easier for the witness to read in Croatian, just to bring the exhibit on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to save time, Your Honour. It's a short passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. If could guide us to the page, and, of course, it would be preferable if the witness -- I was just about to ask you what page you are quoting from, and that usually doesn't take much time to have it on the screen. You can continue meanwhile, and then if the witness wants to look at it, she can.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. It is D1454, page 8 in the English and page 24 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while this is coming up on the screen, Mr. Granic says: "We will not have another opportunity as good as this one when Bihac is still in vital danger. Everything has fallen into place. Everything concerning Srebrenica, Zepa, the Split declaration, the success concerning the Federation, Bihac in danger, the unsuccessful talks, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Granic also refers to a broader context.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to turn to the political and military situation that prevailed at the time that President Tudjman decided not to use military force in Sector East. And I believe you stated in your statement that there was a contemplated operation by the name of Operation Long Jump. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you also referred in your statement to the fact that Sector East was somewhat integrated into the FRY. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was fully integrated into Yugoslavia, completely integrated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the army of the FRY, the VJ, that was a much more powerful force than the ARSK, right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And a conflict between the HV and the VJ would have been a much more serious, at least, a very different matter than a conflict between the HV and the ARSK; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about a conflict in the eastern part of Croatia, it would have been terrible, and it would have had some terrible consequences.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this was a factor for President Tudjman, was it not, the risk that a military operation in Sector East would engage Serbia militarily and would have had these terrible consequences that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he became president, Franjo Tudjman was a general, and he was very familiar with the situation and the manner of warfare in that area and the consequences that would arise. There were those in Croatia who did wish to take the military way of resolving the matter of Eastern Slavonia. However, he didn't permit that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it's right, is it not, that President Tudjman while he was sure that an attack on the Krajina, on Sectors North and South would not result in a conflict with Serbia, he thought that a conflict in Sector East probably would engage Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all of our information, it seemed as if Milosevic would not give up the eastern part of Croatia at any cost. However, with the signing of the Erdut Agreement -- first the Dayton Agreement and then as part of that a little later, the signing of the Erdut Agreement, it all changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like if we can turn briefly to P470. Did you know, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, that President Tudjman met with senior military and Ministry of Defence officials, including General Gotovina, General Cervenko, and Minister Susak on the 26th of September, 1995, to discuss a possible military operation in Eastern Slavonia, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I know of that meeting? I probably did. I didn't know what actually was the content of the meeting, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 90 in the English and page 109 in the B/C/S. I believe it's at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, is where the president speaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And there President Tudjman says: "Wait and let me tell you about Knin and about everything we did. I was sure that there would be no diversion by Serbia and Yugoslavia. But here we need to count that there will be such a diversion. I didn't, please ... I'll do everything so that there is no such diversion, but probably there will be one. So, that's an important difference." Were you aware of this important difference, as President Tudjman described it, between Operation Storm and a possible military operation in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can testify only about the conversations that I had with the president when he explained to me why the military option was not used, because I was supposed to then go on and explain that to others. And it was very logical to me, and clear, even though a very small number of people at that time, in 1995, understood what we were saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you also aware that there was intense pressure placed on Croatia diplomatically, particularly by the United States, not to engage in a military conflict in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there quite a few conversations on that topic. The US of A, at the request of Croatia, were largely involved in finding the solution for Eastern Slavonia, and that was one of the prerequisites enshrined in Dayton, which is to have a new mission after Operation Storm, to which Croatia agreed, and that it be headed by an American, American general, or, rather, just an American, in order to make sure that the mission would be implemented within the set time-limit, that is to say, one year plus one year, which makes a total of two years, and that everything envisaged in the Erdut [indiscernible] would be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to just back up in a time a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P449.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a meeting, a transcript of a meeting that President Tudjman had with Mr. Holbrooke, General Wesley Clark, and Ambassador Galbraith. And do you recall such a meeting on the 18th [Realtime transcript read in error "19th"] of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you were not present; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to page 4 of the English and page 31 in the B/C/S. I believe the transcript should be corrected; I may have misspoke. The meeting was the 18th of August, 1995, at line 22, page 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And here I'd like to look at what Mr. Holbrooke says, which I think is a little to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S. And he says: "I understand, I would like to be very honest, because our administration has been giving you different signals about military activity in the past months. In November, we asked you not to attack, and you did not. In March I flew over here and we agreed, and then you and Gore announced it in Copenhagen, and did you not attack. But then the war started again. And when the war started again and when you went into Western Slavonia, both Ambassador Galbraith and I realized the strategic importance of that operation and the pressure it imposed on the Serbs. So in Washington we adamantly maintained that we should show understanding for the military operation, although we pointed out the right of the Croatian people." If we can go, then, to the next page in the English in page 32, and the next page also in the B/C/S. I think it's at the bottom of the B/C/S. And then he refers to the talks prior to Operation Storm. He says: "Peter was involved in talks with Babic about the Z-4 plan. There was much confusion. You went ahead. It was a triumph from a political and military point of view. And he used the situation again, he helped again. The only problem are the refugees. If you could bring back those people, if you could hold a speech and say that the war is over, to return. Most of them will not return but tell them to return, emphasise it, at least mention they should return ..." If we could go to the next page in the B/C/S. And -- President Tudjman says: "I would very content if about 10 percent of them returned." And Mr. Holbrooke says: "All right. Tell them to return, give them compensation. But if we leave aside the human issue for a minute, I will never forget it, but let's leave it aside for now, you again helped the situation. I would like to make myself clear, since I told you how I feel, secretly and in my heart, which is that you did great things to help peace. I not feel the same about Sector East, Eastern Slavonia. I am firmly convinced that this would be a different situation because it is on the Serbian border ..." And if we could go down to the bottom of the page in the English and to page 34 in the B/C/S, President Tudjman responded and says: "All right, I agree, I am ready -- I am really for a peaceful solution." Mr. Holbrooke says: "I know you are." President Tudjman says: "You know 200 of my men have been killed ... 1400 have been wounded. And if I can effect a peaceful solution, fine. Although the entire Croatian public opinion and the army, they are all ready to move ..." And Mr. Holbrooke says: "Of course, you know. If you attack in Sector East and Milosevic stays out of the conflict, you will win. However, we think he will not be able to stay out." And President Tudjman says: "I know." Does this conversation reflect the military and diplomatic situation at the time, as you recall it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this is a confirmation of what I have already told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you were directly involved in the negotiations of Eastern Slavonia. That's the way you have explained that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And those negotiations involved Ambassador Galbraith and Mr. Stoltenberg; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I think you've mentioned it resulted in the signing of the Erdut Agreement, and that was on the 12th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. On the 12th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Sarinic, the chief negotiator of Croatia, he was the lead negotiator on your side, on the Croatian side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if I may interrupt you, the Chamber has now listened for quite a while to what considerations led to what to do and what not to do in Eastern Slavonia, which I wouldn't say is of no relevance at all, but if it has relevance, it is marginal. The Chamber, therefore, wonders how much further details would assist it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it does have some relevance, and I believe it will become clear. I would be happy to address the Chamber outside the presence of the witness on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then let's move to the point. And let's try to then focus on what your point is. For the Chamber it is not clear at this moment what point of such relevance that would justify such a lot of time to be spent on it is at stake.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then please come to your point as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, these negotiations were ostensibly with the Serbs on the -- in the Eastern Slavonia area, but it is true that Mr. Milosevic had a greet deal of influence over these negotiations on the Serb side. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of conversations between Hrvoje Sarinic and Milosevic in the period up to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in those conversations, Mr. Sarinic sought to secure a deal with Mr. Milosevic that would minimise the number of Serbs remaining in Eastern Slavonia and in Croatia, more generally, including through a eventual exchange of populations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. There was no minimum number of Serbs in Eastern Slavonia agreed. I had very strict instruction from the president of the state, after I had asked him what was I to do in this situations, and how can I do my job if we had nearly 120.000 Serbs and as many Croats had to be brought back? I asked him how was I going to do that, and he painted a very clear picture for me -- excuse me, let me just finish. I think that would be my answer to your question. All the indigenous Serbian population had to remain where they were at any cost. However, those who had come from other parts Croatia, particularly from the Knin area, should return there. And as for those who had come from Serbia and Republika Srpska were to go back to Yugoslavia, Serbia, and Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said you knew that Mr. Sarinic was engaged in talks with Mr. Milosevic. Are you saying that he never discussed population exchanges between Serbs in Eastern Slavonia and Croats in the Vojvodina, or are you saying you don't know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question was that they discussed a minimum number of Serbs, which is not true. They discussed the manner in which these people should be moved, particularly in the way that I just described.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look at what they in fact said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that's at P465.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is a transcript of a meeting on the 29th of August, 1995. It's between President Tudjman and Mr. Sarinic. And in this meeting, Mr. Sarinic describes a meeting he had with Mr. Milosevic about finding a solution for Eastern Slavonia. Did you know about this meeting, either the one with Mr. Milosevic, or the one he had subsequently with President Tudjman describing that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of a lot of meetings, but you will understand that it was impossible for me to know what was discussed at each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, if we could go page 6 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if would you have said at line 15, page 28, P465, and then would have mentioned the page immediately, then we would have had it on the screen already. Now we have to wait until it is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I did want to give the witness a chance to see the cover page of the details of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, here Mr. Sarinic is describing his meeting with Mr. Milosevic. And he said: "Now you know that I told you last time about his view concerning the solution for Eastern Slavonia, that all those who are there should remain there. This time, he said himself that we had to find a solution there and proposed the following, which is an improvement on what was before, but still is not the best. He said like this, all those that came from outside should leave, all Croatian refugees must return. He said those that are there now, what can I do? I can't expel them now, et cetera, let there be a period of time until it all settles down and we will see then." When Mr. Sarinic is referring to Milosevic's earlier position that all those who are there should remain there, he's referring to Milosevic's view that all Serbs then living in Eastern Slavonia should stay. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then when he refers to Milosevic's new proposal, that all those from outside should leave, that's a reference to a new proposal that the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia who are not from there would leave Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's correct. The people who arrived with the army, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page of the English, and page 8 in the B/C/S. I think it's at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And President Tudjman here says: "However, did you really mention that we could do it? Exchange the Croats from Vojvodina?" Turn the page in the B/C/S. And Mr. Sarinic says: "Absolutely, he agreed. At one point I told him ..." And President Tudjman says: "All right. Tell me in an orderly way." Now this is a reference to a proposal that Mr. Sarinic gave to Mr. Milosevic that the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia would be exchanged for Croats in the Vojvodina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the -- you have taken out of the context of the whole picture. At the time the Croats in Serbia were in a rather bad situation. They were being expelled; they were being intimidated; and they, themselves, were looking for a way out of Vojvodina. One part of the Serbian population did not want to stay in Eastern Slavonia under any circumstances. Therefore, a proposal was made to carry out the relocation in a humane manner of all those who couldn't or wouldn't live any longer in their homelands. So this issue was about a humane relocation, not a forced one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could now look at a meeting that was held the following day, which is P466.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it's page 4 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at this meeting, President Tudjman is discussing a possible proposal for Eastern Slavonia with a larger circle of advisors, including Mr. Granic, Mr. Jarnjak, Mr. Milas, Mr. Sarinic, Mr. Pasalic, Mr. Valentic, Mr. Sokol, and Mr. Zuzul. And I'd like to start where Mr. Valentic is speaking. He says: "I do not know much about these problems, but I know from our department, because it is often mentioned that there is a big number of Serbs from Western Slavonia that live in the area of Baranja and Vukovar (around 30.000 of them). So it means that we should expect the request for their return to Western Slavonia." And President Tudjman says: "That is a special problem, and we are going to concentrate on it."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the English. Mr. Valentic responds, and then President Tudjman says: "The next thing I wanted to say is that we should and we could put it like this. Serbs that came from Bosnia and from other places, they should leave, yes." And Mr. Valentic says: "What? Together with our Serbs?" When he says "our Serbs," that's a reference to Croatian Serbs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And President Tudjman says: "Together with our Serbs, and we have to be very flexible about it because of the international community, we should suggest to replace them with Croats in Vojvodina and Serbia (but we cannot write it down) ..." And Mr. Milas says: "Why? That option has always [sic] been carried out after the war." President Tudjman: "Look, it is better not to complicate life for them and for us." And Mr. Milas says: "That is a so-called option that exists in all the international agreements after the First World War." Mr. Valentic says: "I think the most of them will do it, but that should be done in a clever way, and I'm getting in touch with them. As far as I know, Serbs, and I know them well, 80 percent of them will leave." Then at the bottom of the speech he says: "And I'm not afraid that a lot of them will stay, but I also do not agree that we should suggest the exchange immediately but we should try to play a certain game on a long ball, to say in sports terms." And President Tudjman says: "Yes, but we have to suggest it, that the question is open and they are asking it here." Ms. Skare Ozbolt, this conversation reflects the policy of the leadership to try to minimise the number of Serbs remaining in Eastern Slavonia in the context of these negotiations, including through an eventual exchange of populations. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, as you put it, to minimise the number of Serbs does not reflect the situation, because that would involve expulsion of Serbs. The issue here is, and I have to emphasise this, about the Serbs who refused adamantly to stay in Croatia. So this was nothing about minimizing the number of Serbs. This is about those who absolutely did not want to live in Croatia, and you cannot force anyone to stay and live there, if they didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Skare Ozbolt, in this meeting, they're not talking about accommodating people who are desperate to leave Croatia, are they? And whether you call it expulsion, exchange, or humane relocation, this conversation is about a policy of minimizing the number of Serbs remaining in Eastern Slavonia in the negotiations, is it not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the purpose and the meaning of this conversation. I know what was going on. This absolutely does not mean to minimise the number of Serbs in this conversation. They discussed what would happen with the areas once a certain number of Serbs leave. I say again that not all the ideas were brilliant. There were very stupid ideas proffered by the people sitting around the president. But let me tell you again, there was no mention of minimizing the number of Serbs in the aftermaths of Operation Flash, and we are talking about Eastern Slavonia, not western.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There may have been a miscommunication. I was referring to Eastern Slavonia, not Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we are talking about now about Western Slavonia. Western Slavonia. In this transcript, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Valentic raised the problem of Eastern Slavonian Serbs wanting to return to Western Slavonia. Isn't that right? We can go back to the page.

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So they're talking about the return of Serbs to Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that was one part of it that was mentioned. And then President Tudjman said: "In more general terms, we should put it like this, Serbs that came from Bosnia and from other places, they should leave." And Mr. Valentic said: "What? Together with our Serbs?" And President Tudjman said: "Together with our Serbs" --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who wished to leave of their own volition.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is that your personnel interpretation of what President Tudjman is saying there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you weren't at this meeting, and you don't --

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I didn't attend this meeting, but I draw my statement from my personal knowledge. I was given specific tasks that had to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am looking at the clock. I know that Mr. Kehoe wanted to raise something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will first ask the witness to already start having a break, and then we will he hear from Mr. Kehoe. We will resume most likely at five minutes to 11.00, close to 11.00. Madam Usher, will you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The moment has passed and -- with regard to the talking about D422, I do recall Your Honour cautioning us during cross-examination about putting things in context when we pluck things out, and I fully accepted Your Honours' guidance in that regard. And giving the full context of what was happening with this piece of property, the Prosecution sees fit to focus on Article 8, when in fact Article 7 and Article 8 are together and are referenced together as to what is happening to that property. And my question or my objection was in fairness to the witness, reading what those two Articles which clearly go together to give the full context of what is going on, I will cover it in re-examination. But that was my position at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my questions were about prohibitions on the owners of property from selling that property. Article 7 is about prohibitions on the sale of property to the people who had been granted temporary use of that property. I don't think there was any misrepresentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will cover it. I mean, clearly what was contemplated or the line of questioning was the taking of the property by the Croatian government and just giving it to these people. Now whether or not we think this was a right way do it, when these people housed them, they couldn't sell or dispense with any of that property nor could the people who owned the property until they went back to this commission. So it was on equal footing that they tried to have this commission to organise this thing and people that were in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What commission you're talking about now? Let's have the exhibit on the screen so that I can look at it bit better. It was D ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is D422.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence of the witness was that this commission was created in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was therefore asking what commission we were talking about. Could we have it on the screen. Seven and eight. Okay. If you would give me time to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at 4 initially because 4 sets up the commission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I asked to have an opportunity first to read 7 and 8. And I appreciate your suggestion that I should read 4 as well, but I did not invite you to explain 4 to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed -- I'll proceed. Apparently you were referring to the commission mentioned in Article 4, which was a commission set up by the local authorities. Whereas, apparently, you, Ms. Gustafson, were referring to a commission which was created in 1998. Apparently you were talking about two different commissions. So if we first try to avoid that, by the same name, we are talking about different institutions. It is my recollection that the witness yesterday emphasised -- well, quite a bit, on that owners were free to sell either to the state or to others. I think by focussing on Article 8 of this law, Ms. Gustafson was challenging that the freedom to sell was as unrestricted or, let's say, as complete as the witness testified about yesterday; and another matter, which complicates, is that the situation apparently changed after decision of the constitutional court, which means that we have to consider what was place in 1995, 1996, 1997, and then, as the witness drew our attention to, that situations changed in 1998. And that appears to be the situation. Now, to say that if the witness so much has drawn our attention to the freedom to sell to whomever, then to require from Ms. Gustafson to put the full picture again, also the rights of those who were housed in these properties that they were not able to sell, that, of course, would complete the picture, to the extent the Chamber was not able to read that themselves. Not everything that is in documents should always be put completely to a witness. If it would be unfair to a witness to do it, then, of course, can ask to give a better context. But in view of the testimony of the witness yesterday, which was about the rights of owners to sell to whomever they wanted to sell, I think it was not inappropriate to focus, as Ms. Gustafson did, on Article 8. Let's not -- let try to elicit from the witness the evidence which you, Mr. Kehoe, or you, Ms. Gustafson, consider important. Let's try to refrain from unnecessarily interfering, if the other party is eliciting that evidence. The complete picture we'll have at the end of the testimony as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and even with the microphone, I would hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the microphone off, I appreciate your guidance. And my sole issue in standing up at that time is -- and asking for the full picture is that it started off with property -- Ms. Gustafson referring to this as property confiscation. And that's why I thought the full picture [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, but we have a lot of semantic issues. What does mean minimise the population? If you say I would like to say 10 percent of Serbs, is that minimizing? Of course not. Because 2 percent is even less; 5 percent is less; 9 percent is less. So minimizing, it's a word. Confiscation, of course, should be understood in this context as, that's at least how I understood it, that you're deprived of the ownership rights without getting an acceptable amount of money for it, and whether that would be forever or for 30 years or for three years, or just until the constitutional court decides on a matter. Otherwise, or up to the moment that the constitutional or any other court would then change that again, that's -- we are no imbeciles. At least I hope that we didn't give that you impression. If someone is using the word "confiscation," then, of course, this is understood in the context. And if you would look at confiscation, will you see that in the many legal systems that it -- it's different anywhere, confiscation here as a punishment, confiscation as a matter of protecting state interests, confiscation -- well, that's -- it was perfectly clear, we do not focus on the word "confiscation" and then start a comparative legal study on the word confiscation. We are talking, it's short for what Ms. Gustafson finds in this law. And, of course, we'll not take it for granted what Ms. Gustafson -- what the use of the word. I mean, Ms. Gustafson today talked about the attack on the Krajina. We could spend half an hour at least on whether regaining territorial control of an area, is that attack, is that not attack? We -- we understand the language Ms. Gustafson uses and you use, in its context, and we hope that the parties have at least some confidence in that we'll do that, because, if not, I'll have to report to the President that this case will take twice as long as it is scheduled for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At caution, Judge. The benefit of the doubt goes to the Chamber. It couldn't take twice as long. Just kidding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're just kidding. Even that -- Mr. Kehoe, I said we were are no imbeciles, that you were kidding was already understood by us. So no need to explain that. We'll have a break, and we will resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Ms. Gustafson, just a short procedural matter. A request has been filed for videolink evidence for Witness AG-61, 15th of June. The Chamber understands that all parties agreed that we could hear the evidence in one day, and that the parties agreed on timing, and it's on that basis, if it is not correctly understood, please tell it now or be silent forever. On that basis, the Chamber grants the request for videolink. A formal decision will follow. There is also a still pending motion for a subpoena, in relation to that same witness. The Chamber will put that motion on hold, on the basis that, in the request for the videolink, it was expressed that the witness would voluntarily appear for the videolink. At the same time, we withdraw it now not knowing what the future will bring us might not be very wise. But that's the reason, why the Chamber, at this moment, does not decide on that motion, most likely later to be declared moot or to be withdrawn. Having dealt with this procedural matter, Ms. Gustafson, if you are ready to proceed, please do so. The Chamber would like to add some concerns about the interrupted flow of evidence but also had some concerns on how quickly you went to the core of the issue. What took approximately 20 minutes, if not more, the Chamber thought that it -- you might have reached the same point, and the point, of course, is perfectly clear, in five to ten minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Skare Ozbolt, I'd like to ask you now about your negotiations in respect of Eastern Slavonia. And the -- in the course of these negotiations, the Croatian leadership was concerned that the terms of this deal might enable the return of Serbs to the Krajina, and you and Mr. Sarinic sought a deal that would prevent such a return. That was the negotiating position you took; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our negotiating position was that Serbs in -- or from the Krajina should return to the Krajina, to the place of their residence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to Exhibit P458, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In these negotiations had you quite a few discussions with Ambassador Galbraith, is that right, you and Mr. Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 46 in the English and the fourth translation in B/C/S of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is Ambassador Galbraith's diplomatic diary. And this particular passage is an entry from the 15th of September. And it says: "We had a long conversation about the return of refugees. Sarinic initially was hard-line. He was also concerned about the impact of demographic change in Sector East if the Krajina Serbs and west Slavonia Serbs stayed there. I pointed out that in connection with the Western Slavonia Serbs, he had said that they could stay or return to their homes in Western Slavonia. He replied that that was six months ago and things had changed. "I said strongly that the US could only support a settlement that involved the right of Croatian citizens who are Serbs to remain in Croatia and to return to their homes wherever they are in Croatia." Now further down, in the next paragraph he says: "He then said that the key was whether the Croats could get their property back in Sector East. If so, the danger of too many out of area Serbs settling there was less. I said that the Eastern Slavonia Serbs have already agreed to this. But any settlement would have to provide for the right of all Croatian citizens, Croats and Serbs" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, could we just go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me, if we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "... to recover their property and to return home. He smiled and said, I expected you to say this." Now, this entry reflects Ambassador Galbraith's insistence that Croatian citizens should have the right to return to their homes wherever they are in Croatia, and Mr. Sarinic is resisting that idea. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Sarinic was not against the return of everyone to their own home. After all, that was the policy that we implemented, that everyone should return to their own home. At the time, a large number of refugees from the Krajina came to Eastern Slavonia and the Krajina government was providing assurance to them when they left Krajina that Eastern Slavonia would be their new permanent place of residence. So people believed that they would remain there permanently. You have evidence of that in numerous public statements on television. Serbs from Krajina stated this; simply, there had to be some kind of order imposed in the region of Eastern Slavonia. Later, the procedure, everyone to their own homes, was completed implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Sarinic was concerned that during the transition period in Eastern Slavonia, Serbs from the Krajina would be packed into Eastern Slavonia and, from there, would eventually be able to return to the Krajina, and you and he sought to prevent that. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not preventing anything in the transition period. We implemented the return of everyone to their own home. Those who lived from Krajina, from Knin, who lived in the eastern parts of Croatia, returned --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going interrupt you because my question was not about what happened in the transition period. My question was about Mr. Sarinic's concerns during the negotiations --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 54 in the English and the sixth translation in the B/C/S in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is an entry from the 22nd of September, which was -- do you recall a draft plan for Eastern Slavonia being presented to you by Ambassador Galbraith around this time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: What draft plan? I don't know. There was -- the only draft plan for Eastern Slavonia was the Erdut Agreement. There was no other draft agreement, or draft plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in this entry Ambassador Galbraith is referring to a draft. Perhaps you didn't see it. And he says: "I presented the Eastern Slavonia plan to Sarinic, both the outlying memo and the detailed plan. He reacted angrily, I think particularly set off by the word "autonomy" in the outline memo. His real concern is that the plan would enable the Krajina Serbs to return to Croatia through the back door of Eastern Slavonia, not only changing the ethnic balance there but undoing the ethnic purification of Operation Storm. Politely I told him, Tough. Croatia will have to accept the return of its citizens and the implementation of its constitution." This entry, reflects, does it not, Mr. Sarinic's concern that the proposal Galbraith presented to him would allow Krajina Serb refugees to pack into Sector East and eventually return home, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to note here that this is the 22nd of September. At the time, there were discussions about an agreement that would later be called the Erdut Agreement. Peter Galbraith here does not give up his Z-4 plan, and he mentioned the word "autonomy" there. However, that was probably something that upset Hrvoje Sarinic, to the point that he showed it. At the time, when the Erdut Agreement was talked about, we did not talk about people who were expelled. We sought a legal framework for bringing things into order and how to fulfil everything that had to be fulfilled within a two-year period, ranging from the demilitarization to reintegration, and reconciliation. At the time, it was absolutely not a topic of discussion, the return of everyone to their own home.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll, let's look at one more entry, which is at page 60 of the English. And it is the second-last translation in the B/C/S. And this is now the 2nd of October. And it says: "I flew back and immediately went to see Sarinic. He was difficult on the principles, and, in particular, on the human rights issues. He wanted it to be clear that the right of return applied only to Sector East and not more generally, arguing this was an agreement about Sector East only. Once again, his real concern is that the Serbs could pack Sector East with Krajina refugees. I said the Sector East Serbs would not want to share, but also that Croatia could not escape its human rights obligations. Croatia, I said, had accepted the right of return, and in point 6, the highest levels of internationally recognised human rights. People were free to settle where they wanted. Vesna said this was before the war. I pointed out that Tudjman had told Clinton during the war that Croatia would respect human rights." That reference to Vesna, that would be a reference to you, right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... do you recall saying that to Ambassador Galbraith, that people, when he said people were free to settle where they wanted, you said, That was before the war?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our discussion was much longer than this one sentence, and I very clearly told him and I remember that, that when everyone returned to their own home, then after that, they could move wherever they wished. But before that, we needed to re-establish the situation that prevailed before the war, before 1991. That was supposed to be the sense of this conversation that we had, and it was the sense of the conversation. And we absolutely guaranteed, and that's how it turned out to be, that Croatia would respect the Article guaranteeing human rights. Absolutely no one, however, was able allow that people simply who had been expelled or for whatever reason had left, began to move wherever they wished in Croatia. They could only do that once they had returned to their original place of residence. After that, they could move wherever they wanted to in Croatia. So the essence was to re-establish the situation, as it was, before 1991. After everyone returned to their own home, then they could move anywhere in Croatia that they wished. That was the gist of the discussion. And that is what Vesna said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you said those words to Ambassador Galbraith, right, that was before the war?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used the same words to Ambassador Galbraith that I told you now, but he took them out of context, and the fact that this sounds like this, the way it does, in his diary, is a thing for him. I mean, it's his diary. But now that I have clarified, this is the context that this was stated in. I did provide an explanation now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And even after the Erdut Agreement was signed, President Tudjman's policy towards the Krajina Serbs who had left Croatia was that they could not return to Croatia, at least not in any significant number. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 7253, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you recall President Tudjman delivering a speech in Vukovar, around the 8th of June, 1997?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were you at that speech?

utterances.speaker: VESNA SKARE OZBOLT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of the English, and I believe page 3 of the B/C/S; I'll just check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the top of page in the B/C/S, you see President Tudjman stating: "Ladies and gentlemen, all those Serbs who are citizens of Croatia, who have taken Croatian citizenship and who are living in this country and the neighbouring Osijek-Baranja -- sorry, this county and the neighbouring Osijek-Baranja county and the entire Danubian area, if they want to return to their homes in the western parts of Croatia from Pakrac to Knin, they will be allowed to return. About 14.500 have already returned. If they do not want to return, we shall give them compensation so that they can go wherever they wish. "Out of humanitarian reasons, Croatia will resolve individual cases of Serbs who fled Croatia, despite the fact that I, as president, personally invited them to stay. Out of humanitarian reasons, we will resolve their cases so they can return to Croatia to rejoin their families.
